instructional_purpose: Trains parse-time disambiguation of a single very high-frequency form (ما) that carries nine distinct grammatical roles, so that a reader assigns the role from surrounding syntactic evidence rather than from a default gloss. Supplies an ordered diagnostic path plus a role-by-role parsing template.
concepts_taught: inventory of nine grammatical roles carried by one surface form
plain verbal negation that contributes no governance
dialect-marked negation that behaves like a copula-negator (nominative subject, accusative predicate)
relative-noun use requiring a linking pronoun back to the head
masdar-forming use yielding an interpreted verbal noun
exclamatory template built on a frozen verb plus accusative object of wonder
interrogative use and its vowel-shortened form after prepositions
conditional use that puts both protasis and apodosis verbs in the jussive
expletive attachment (governance preserved) versus preventive attachment (governance cancelled)
combination with a defective verb of the كان family to build a duration clause
ordered decision procedure over the nine roles

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The plain negating use exerts no governance: the negated verb keeps exactly the inflection it would have without the negator.

The dialect-marked negating variant assigns nominative to the subject and accusative to the predicate, but only when the predicate is not fronted, not preceded by an exception particle, and not followed by a conditional particle.
The negating use attaches to past-tense verbs.
Presence of a returning pronoun distinguishes the relative use from the masdar-forming use, and absence of one plus substitutability by an explicit masdar identifies the masdar-forming use.
In the exclamatory template the form is an inchoative subject and the frozen verb carries a concealed pronoun subject referring to it.

The preventive attachment cancels the accusative-assigning power of the emphatic particle and the genitive-assigning power of the ratio particle; the expletive attachment leaves the host's governance intact; one and the same compound may fall on either side depending on context.
Loss of the long vowel after a preposition is a reliable signature of the interrogative use.
The conditional use imposes the jussive on both clause verbs and itself occupies a fronted object position.
The lesson's decision path files the dialect-marked nominal-clause negation under a branch whose test is 'the following verb is past tense', which cannot be applied as written.

recognition_criteria: what immediately follows: verb versus noun versus nothing (host-attached)
tense/mood of the following verb, and whether the mood is jussive
presence or absence of a pronoun in the following clause that points back to the form
case marking on a following predicate in a nominal clause (accusative signals the dialect-marked negator)
identity of the host particle when the form is suffixed to another particle
loss of the long vowel when the form follows a preposition
the fixed exclamatory template shape (frozen verb plus accusative)
substitutability of the form-plus-verb string by an explicit verbal noun
procedures: Step 1: check whether a verb follows; if not, consider interrogative use or host-attached use.
Step 2: if a past verb follows, sort among plain negation, masdar-forming use after a temporal head, and the exclamatory template by looking at the template shape and the preceding word.
Step 3: if an imperfective follows, use jussive mood to select the conditional use, a returning pronoun to select the relative use, and masdar substitutability to select the masdar-forming use.
Step 4: if the form is suffixed to another particle, decide expletive versus preventive by whether the host still assigns its case.
Step 5: if the form follows a preposition in shortened shape, read it as interrogative.
Per-role parsing template: state role label, indeclinability, and either 'no syntactic position' (particle roles) or the positional case with its function (noun roles).
conditions: dialect-marked negation governs only under its three ordering/blocking conditions
the conditional use requires both verbs to be capable of jussive marking
the masdar-forming reading requires an environment where a verbal noun could stand (typically after a temporal head or a governing verb)
the preventive reading requires a host particle that otherwise assigns a case
exceptions: a compound host particle may take either the expletive or the preventive analysis, so the compound alone does not fix the reading
the relative use may lack an overt returning pronoun when the head fills the subject slot of its own clause
the duration construction pairs the form with a defective verb, so the whole string, not the form alone, carries the temporal sense
contrasts: plain negation (no governance) versus dialect-marked negation (assigns nominative and accusative)
relative use (returning pronoun, replaceable by a definite relative noun) versus masdar-forming use (no returning pronoun, replaceable by an explicit masdar)
expletive attachment (host governance preserved) versus preventive attachment (host governance cancelled)
duration construction with a defective verb versus negation of a re-inception verb, which look alike on the surface but differ in role
particle roles with no syntactic position versus noun roles that occupy a positional case

common_mistakes.pattern: Assigning the relative reading where the masdar-forming reading is correct, and the reverse.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Both roles sit in front of a verb, so surface order does not separate them.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Apply the substitution test: if the string can be replaced by an explicit verbal noun with meaning preserved, the role is masdar-forming; if a linking pronoun is present or recoverable, it is relative.

common_mistakes.pattern: Leaving both verbs in the indicative under the conditional use.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The conditional use is jussive-assigning, so indicative marking violates its governance.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Mark protasis and apodosis verbs jussive whenever the conditional reading is selected.

common_mistakes.pattern: Applying the emphatic particle's accusative assignment after the preventive attachment.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The attached element cancels the host's case assignment, so the following noun stays nominative.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Once the preventive analysis is chosen, drop the host's governance from the parse entirely.

common_mistakes.pattern: Reading the exclamatory template compositionally as a question or as an ordinary past-verb clause.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The template is frozen; its verb is not a free lexical past verb and its complement is not an ordinary object of inquiry.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Recognize the fixed template shape as a unit before parsing its parts.

misleading_shortcuts: treating the form as a negator by default because negation is its most frequent role
assuming an accusative predicate after the form always signals the dialect-marked negator without checking the blocking conditions
assuming the compound spellings always carry the preventive analysis
assuming the presence of a following verb settles the role

state the role label and indeclinable base

nahw_relevance: high — governance, mood assignment, positional case and clause typing all turn on which role is selected.

Role assignment without at least one of these is not licensed.

instructional_purpose: Trains four-way role disambiguation of the short subordinating particle أنْ, using what precedes it and what follows it as joint evidence, and connects each role to its governance consequence (subjunctive assignment, no assignment, or none at all).
concepts_taught: four grammatical roles of one short subordinator
masdar-forming role that assigns the subjunctive and yields an interpreted verbal noun
lightened role derived from the heavy emphatic particle, with an unexpressed pronoun-of-the-matter as its subject
explanatory role after verbs of speech, signalling and writing, introducing the content of the signal
expletive role with no grammatical effect
governing-verb classes that select each role (volition/attempt/fear versus knowledge/certainty versus speech/signalling)

combination with prepositions and temporal heads to build purpose, priority and posteriority phrases
juncture vowel appearing on the particle before a vowel-initial word

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The masdar-forming role assigns the subjunctive to the following imperfective and the resulting string occupies a nominal position (subject, object or genitive complement).
The lightened role is the heavy emphatic particle with its gemination removed, its subject noun being an unexpressed pronoun of the matter, and the following clause serving as its predicate.
The lightened role assigns no mood; it is instead signalled by a following negator, perfective marker, future marker or jussive negator.

The semantic class of the preceding verb selects the role: volition/attempt/fear verbs select the masdar-forming role, knowledge/certainty verbs select the lightened role, speech/signalling verbs select the explanatory role.
The explanatory role carries no syntactic position and is normally followed by an imperative or a prohibition.
The expletive role can be deleted with no change in grammaticality or propositional meaning, while adding emphasis or immediacy.
Removability with meaning preserved is a decisive test for the expletive role, and replaceability by an explicit verbal noun is a decisive test for the masdar-forming role.
The lesson explicitly walls off the heavy geminate emphatic particle as out of scope, treating only the light form and its lightened descendant.

recognition_criteria: mood of the following imperfective (subjunctive marking, including loss of the plural/feminine ending letter)
presence of a negator, perfective marker, future marker or jussive negator directly after the particle
presence of an imperative or prohibition directly after the particle
semantic class of the verb immediately preceding the particle
presence of a temporal head or a preposition immediately before the particle
juncture vowel on the particle before a vowel-initial word
procedures: Look right first: subjunctive imperfective points to the masdar-forming role; negator/perfective/future/jussive-negator points to the lightened role; imperative points to the explanatory role; a past verb after a temporal head points to the expletive role.
Look left second: volition/attempt/fear verbs, knowledge/certainty verbs, speech/signalling verbs and temporal heads each bias a different role.
Apply the substitution test: replace the particle plus verb by an explicit verbal noun; success confirms the masdar-forming role.
Apply the deletion test: remove the particle; if grammaticality and meaning survive, the role is expletive.

Assign the parse: for the masdar-forming role state the subjunctive marker and then the positional case of the whole interpreted noun; for the lightened role state the unexpressed subject and the clause as its predicate; for the explanatory and expletive roles state that the particle has no syntactic position.
conditions: subjunctive assignment holds only for the masdar-forming role
the lightened reading requires a preceding predicate of knowledge or certainty plus one of its following markers
the explanatory reading requires a preceding speech/signalling predicate that is not introducing a direct quotation
compound purpose and time phrases require the masdar-forming role, since the interpreted noun is what the preposition or temporal head governs
exceptions: the explanatory role's base vowel shifts to a juncture vowel before a vowel-initial word, so the surface shape changes without a change of role
verbs of expectation and advice appear in the lesson on the masdar-forming side even though they are close to the knowledge/speech classes, so the verb-class heuristic is not airtight
the lightened role may be followed by an indicative imperfective, which defeats a mood-only test
contrasts: masdar-forming (assigns subjunctive, substitutable by a verbal noun) versus lightened (assigns nothing, marker-signalled)
masdar-forming (followed by subjunctive) versus explanatory (followed by imperative or prohibition)
explanatory content clause versus direct quotation after a speech verb
expletive (deletable) versus every other role (not deletable)
the light particle versus the heavy geminate emphatic particle it derives from

common_mistakes.pattern: Reading the masdar-forming role where the lightened role holds, typically when a negator follows.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The negator after the particle is a lightened-role marker, and the preceding knowledge predicate confirms it; the masdar-forming reading would wrongly predict a subjunctive verb.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Combine the left-hand verb class with the right-hand marker before assigning the role.

common_mistakes.pattern: Leaving the verb in the indicative after the masdar-forming role.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: That role is a subjunctive assigner, so indicative marking contradicts the parse.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Whenever the masdar-forming role is selected, realize the subjunctive marker on the following verb.

common_mistakes.pattern: Conflating the light particle with the heavy geminate emphatic particle.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: They differ in shape, in what they govern, and in whether they take an explicit accusative subject noun.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Treat gemination as a categorial distinction, and treat the lightened role as the derived, subject-less descendant of the heavy particle.

common_mistakes.pattern: Missing the explanatory structure and parsing an imperative clause as a masdar-forming complement.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The masdar-forming role cannot govern an imperative, and the preceding signalling verb licenses a content clause instead.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: A signalling or speech predicate followed by an imperative selects the explanatory role.

misleading_shortcuts: treating the particle as a uniform infinitive marker because the masdar-forming role is the most frequent
using the semantic class of the preceding verb alone as a decision rule
assuming that any following negator or perfective marker forces the lightened reading regardless of the preceding predicate
assuming a deletable particle is always expletive without checking that the meaning is genuinely unchanged

instructional_purpose: Establishes that the definiteness of a preceding noun, not the shape or tense of the following clause, decides whether that clause is parsed as a circumstantial state or as an attributive modifier, and works out the different case consequences of the two analyses.
concepts_taught: definiteness as the licensing trigger for clause attachment type
clausal circumstantial state after a definite head, fixed in accusative position
clausal attribute after an indefinite head, copying the head's case
the inventory of what counts as definite (proper noun, pronoun, article-marked noun, annexation to a definite term, demonstrative, relative noun)
single-word, nominal-clause and verbal-clause realizations of the circumstantial state
the circumstantial connective particle introducing a state clause
the returning pronoun inside an attributive clause, overt or concealed
the divergence between English translation equivalence and Arabic parse difference

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A clause following a definite noun is parsed as a circumstantial state; a clause following an indefinite noun is parsed as an attribute.
The clausal circumstantial state always occupies accusative position regardless of the case of its head.
The clausal attribute occupies the same positional case as the noun it modifies, so its position varies with the head's case.
Annexation to a definite second term makes the head definite and therefore flips the following clause from attribute to circumstantial state.
An attributive clause contains a pronoun linking back to its head, overt when the head is not the clause's own subject and concealed when it is.

The two constructions are semantically distinguishable: the state answers a manner/condition question about an already-identified referent, while the attribute answers an identifying question about an unidentified one.

The rule is stated without exception classes; in the wider tradition definite heads that are only formally definite, and indefinite heads specialized by modification, are known to complicate it, and the lesson does not address these.
A clause after an indefinite head is treated as distinct in structure from a relative clause introduced by a definite relative noun, even where the English rendering is identical.

recognition_criteria: definiteness status of the immediately preceding noun, checked against the six definiteness sources
whether the head is definite by annexation rather than by article
presence of the circumstantial connective at the head of the following clause
presence and form of a returning pronoun in the following clause
the case borne by the head noun, which the attributive clause must mirror
procedures: Determine the head noun's definiteness first, before looking at the clause at all.
If the head is definite, label the clause a circumstantial state and assign it accusative position irrespective of the head's own case.
If the head is indefinite, label the clause an attribute and assign it the head's case as positional case.
Classify the clause's internal shape (nominal versus verbal) and, for nominal state clauses, identify the circumstantial connective and the resumptive subject pronoun.
Locate the returning pronoun, or state that it is concealed as the clause's own subject.
Write the full parse: head's own case and function, then the clause's positional case and function.
conditions: the head of a circumstantial state must be definite
the head of an attributive clause must be indefinite
case-copying applies only to the attributive analysis; the state analysis is case-invariant
the circumstantial connective typically introduces nominal state clauses; verbal state clauses may stand without it
exceptions: definiteness may come from annexation rather than from the article, which learners routinely overlook
multiple state clauses may stack on a single definite head
the concealed returning pronoun leaves an attributive clause with no visible link to its head
contrasts: definite head plus clause (state, accusative position, case-invariant) versus indefinite head plus clause (attribute, case-copying)
state describing manner/condition versus attribute identifying which referent
attributive clause after an indefinite head versus relative clause after a definite relative noun
single-word state versus nominal-clause state versus verbal-clause state

common_mistakes.pattern: Labelling a clause after a proper noun as an attribute.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Proper nouns are definite, so the licensing rule assigns the state analysis.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Check the full definiteness inventory, not just the presence of the article.

common_mistakes.pattern: Ignoring that annexation to a definite term makes the head definite.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The head looks article-less, so it is misread as indefinite and the clause is misfiled as an attribute.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Resolve annexation before judging definiteness.

common_mistakes.pattern: Assigning the wrong positional case to an attributive clause.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The attributive clause copies its head's case; assigning nominative to a clause modifying a genitive head breaks agreement.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Read the head's case off its governor first, then copy it onto the clause.

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating every clause following any noun as a circumstantial state.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The state analysis is licensed only by a definite head; after an indefinite head it is unlicensed.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Let definiteness, not clause shape, select the analysis.

common_mistakes.pattern: Collapsing the distinction because the English translations coincide.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Translation equivalence is not parse equivalence; case assignment and syntactic function differ.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Parse from the Arabic licensing condition, never from the English rendering.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The expression decomposes into a genus-negating particle plus a noun meaning 'equal' plus a suffixed element, with the predicate of the negation deleted and understood.
A definite complement is genitive as the annexation term of the 'equal' noun.
An indefinite complement admits nominative, accusative and genitive, analysed respectively as predicate of a deleted subject, as specification, and as annexation term; all three are grammatical.
When a full clause follows, the suffixed element cannot be expletive and must be read as a relative noun whose clause is its relative content.
A definite complement in the nominative is also defensible, under the relative reading with a deleted subject, and is attested alongside the genitive.
The nominative is the most frequent option for indefinite complements in classical texts and the specification-accusative is the rarest.
The accusative is not available for a definite complement.
The literal sense 'there is no equal of X' is what motivates the singling-out force of the expression.

recognition_criteria: whether the complement carries the definite article or is a proper name
whether the complement is a bare noun or a full clause containing a verb
the case vowel actually realized on the complement, which selects among competing analyses rather than deciding grammaticality
presence of a conditional or temporal head opening the complement, signalling the clausal pattern
procedures: Check definiteness of the complement: if definite, assign genitive as annexation term (with the nominative variant noted as attested).
If not definite, check whether the complement is a clause: if so, read the suffixed element as a relative noun and the clause as its content.
If the complement is an indefinite noun, choose among three case options and state the analysis matching the chosen case.
Write the parse in layers: genus-negating particle, its subject noun, the status of the suffixed element (expletive or relative), then the complement's case and function.
Note the deleted predicate of the genus negation explicitly rather than leaving it unaccounted.
conditions: the genitive analysis requires the complement to be a bare noun that can serve as an annexation term
the relative analysis of the suffixed element is required, not optional, when a clause follows
the specification analysis requires accusative marking

common_mistakes.pattern: Putting a definite complement in the accusative.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The definite complement is an annexation term, and annexation terms are genitive.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Definite complement selects genitive; accusative is reserved for the specification analysis, which requires an indefinite.

common_mistakes.pattern: Keeping the expletive analysis of the suffixed element when a clause follows.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: An expletive element cannot take a clause as its content, so the clause would be left unattached.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: A following clause forces the relative reading, and the clause is then parsed as the relative content.

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating the three indefinite case options as equally frequent.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Grammatical validity is not distributional equality; the classical texts favour one option and the specification accusative is rare.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Keep validity and frequency as separate judgements when choosing a reading.

common_mistakes.pattern: Confusing the singling-out expression with the exclusion word of opposite sense.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: One highlights a member of the set, the other removes it, so the readings are contradictory.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Fix the semantic direction (inclusion-highlighting versus exclusion) before parsing.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The word is an indeclinable adverb of place whose final vowel is fixed and never varies with the case of its environment.
It must be followed by a complete clause and can never take a bare noun as its complement.
The following clause occupies genitive position as the annexation term, because the adverb functions as the first element of an annexation.
Grammarians justify its indeclinability by its particle-like linking function.
The suffixed conditional derivative assigns the jussive to both the condition verb and the response verb and itself occupies accusative adverbial position.
The returning pronoun is optional after this adverb and surfaces only when the semantic link to the place requires a preposition; definite relative nouns normally require it.
In its abstract respect-marking use the adverb is still followed by a clause, or by a nominal phrase functioning as one.
The lesson's parse of the compound analysis treats the suffixed element in the conditional derivative as expletive while simultaneously calling the whole a jussive-assigning conditional noun.

common_mistakes.pattern: Putting a bare noun after the adverb.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Its complement slot is filled by a clause standing in genitive position; a bare noun leaves the required clause missing.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Expand the intended noun into a full clause, or switch to a relative-noun construction.

common_mistakes.pattern: Changing the adverb's final vowel to match a preceding genitive.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The word is indeclinable, so it does not participate in case marking; only its position varies.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Keep the fixed vowel and express its grammatical role as a positional case instead.

common_mistakes.pattern: Using the place interrogative in a relative-type place expression.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The interrogative belongs to questions and does not license a modifying clause of place.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Use the locative adverb, or a relative noun with a resumptive preposition-plus-pronoun.

common_mistakes.pattern: Leaving the verbs indicative after the suffixed conditional derivative.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: That form is a jussive assigner, so indicative marking contradicts its governance.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Mark both condition and response verbs jussive whenever the conditional form is used.

common_mistakes.pattern: Ending a sentence with the adverb and no following clause.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The annexation is left without its second term.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Supply the clause; the adverb cannot stand alone.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A declinable noun whose final segment cannot bear a vowel still carries case; the case is stated as estimated on that final segment with a named reason.
Indeclinable words carry no case marking at all but occupy case positions, which are stated with the positional formula.
The three reasons for estimated case are impossibility (final long alif), heaviness (final yā' after a kasra) and occupation of the slot by the vowel required to attach the first-person possessive.
Defective nouns in final yā' show a visible accusative while their nominative and genitive are estimated.
Relative content clauses have no positional case at all, unlike clauses filling predicate or modifier slots.

The lesson attributes an estimated nominative on a diptote proper name to heaviness and to diptote status; standard analysis makes the nominative vowel on a diptote fully visible, the diptote effect being loss of nunation and a fatha in place of the genitive kasra.
Names of scriptural origin are said to take estimated case because of their foreign-origin endings; the operative factor is the final segment's shape, not the name's provenance.
One parsing-table row labels a possessed noun in the lesson's passage a direct object with estimated accusative, though its context makes it the second term of an annexation and therefore genitive.

common_mistakes.pattern: Applying the estimated analysis to indeclinable words and the positional analysis to declinable ones.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The two analyses answer different questions: one is about a blocked marker on a word that does inflect, the other about a word that never inflects at all.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Decide inflectional status first; the analysis follows from it.

common_mistakes.pattern: Giving an estimated-case parse without naming the blocking reason.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The reason is part of the required parse; without it the parse does not explain why the vowel is absent.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Always append the named reason appropriate to the final segment.

common_mistakes.pattern: Calling a defective noun indeclinable.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: It is declinable and shows a visible accusative, so it cannot be indeclinable.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Test the accusative form before declaring indeclinability.

common_mistakes.pattern: Using the positional formula for declinable words with blocked marking.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Positional wording asserts the absence of any case marking, which is false for a declinable word.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Reserve positional wording for indeclinables and clauses.

common_mistakes.pattern: Forgetting that clauses filling nominal slots also take positional case.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: A predicate clause occupies a nominative slot and must be parsed as such, not left unanalysed.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Assign clauses a position and function whenever they fill a nominal slot.

instructional_purpose: Establishes that a single well-formed Arabic sentence can carry several fully licensed parses, distinguishes this from vagueness and from error, and supplies the classical preference principles used to rank competing analyses when one must be chosen.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A single sentence may admit several analyses each of which satisfies the grammar, producing different but legitimate meanings.
The accusative marker alone does not determine grammatical function, since several distinct functions share it.
Cognition verbs take one object under a perception reading and two objects under a judgement reading, and this frame choice generates competing parses.
A circumstantial accusative may be referred either to the subject or to the object when both are eligible, with context alone deciding.
Preference among licensed parses is governed by proximity of the modifier to its host, by contextual sense, by attested usage, by scholarly consensus, and by minimizing assumed deleted material.
A parse requiring a deleted copular verb competes with a plain circumstantial parse for the same string, the two differing in implied prior state.
Several readings may be simultaneously intended by an author, so preserving multiplicity can be the correct outcome rather than resolving it.

One exclamatory-versus-interrogative-versus-negative string is offered as admitting three whole-sentence readings, which extends the multiplicity claim from a single element to the entire clause type.

procedures: Enumerate all licensed parses before selecting one, rather than committing to the first reading.
For each candidate, state what the disputed element is analysed as and what meaning follows.
Apply the preference principles in order: nearest host, contextual sense, attested usage, consensus, least assumed deletion.
Decide whether the context genuinely selects one reading or whether the multiplicity is intended and should be preserved.
Record the rejected parses rather than discarding them, since they remain grammatically licensed.

common_mistakes.pattern: Assuming exactly one parse must be correct and the others wrong.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: In genuine multiplicity every candidate satisfies the grammar; the question is contextual fit, not licensing.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Separate the licensing question from the selection question and answer them in that order.

common_mistakes.pattern: Filing multiple licensed parses as a grammatical error.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: An error involves a reading that breaks a rule; multiplicity involves readings that all obey the rules.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Test each candidate against the rules before calling anything an error.

common_mistakes.pattern: Choosing among parses without consulting context.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Licensing is context-free but selection is not; treating all candidates as equally likely discards the strongest evidence available.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Rank licensed candidates by contextual fit, and say which context feature did the work.

common_mistakes.pattern: Preferring the structurally simplest parse automatically.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Assumed deletion is sometimes exactly what the author intended, especially in elevated registers.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Treat simplicity as a tie-break, applied after sense and attestation.

common_mistakes.pattern: Missing the two-frame behaviour of cognition predicates.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Reading a judgement-frame clause as a one-object perception clause leaves the second accusative unaccounted for.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Check the predicate's frame options before assigning roles to accusatives.

role disambiguation of polysemous items by surrounding evidence, established in the earlier particle lessons
new_knowledge: an explicit account of non-unique parsing as a licensed outcome
a ranked tie-break procedure for choosing among licensed parses
the taxonomy of structural sources that generate multiplicity
the principled distinction between multiplicity, vagueness, error and ellipsis
the legitimacy of preserving multiplicity rather than resolving it
later_dependencies: any downstream parsing task that must report analyses rather than a single label
exegetical and commentary reading, where competing readings are recorded side by side
evaluation practice: judging a parse as correct requires knowing whether alternatives were licensed
sarf_relevance: none — the lesson operates entirely on syntactic role assignment; no morphological content.
nahw_relevance: high — it is about the licensing and ranking of competing syntactic analyses, and it directly governs how confidently any single parse may be asserted.
tutor_drill_relevance: high, but only in a format that accepts sets: drills should ask the learner to enumerate licensed parses and justify a ranking, and must not score a licensed alternative as wrong.
rich_hover_relevance: high and cautionary — hover must be able to display more than one licensed analysis with a preference note; a single-label hover on an accusative complement will silently suppress licensed alternatives.
corpus_pvn_relevance: No new headwords. Constrains all three entry kinds at the annotation layer: v entries for cognition predicates need a frame feature (one-object perception versus two-object judgement) and a polysemy flag where the predicate's sense changes the complement's role; n entries in accusative position need a role-set rather than a single role where multiple analyses are licensed.
required_evidence: To assert a unique parse: evidence that competing analyses are unlicensed in this context, not merely unmentioned. Per occurrence this means the predicate's frame options, the eligible hosts for any circumstantial element, the antecedent candidates for any relative clause, and the contextual feature invoked to rank. Absent that, the honest output is a ranked set.
uncertainty_flags: unsafe-for-automatic-projection: any pipeline that emits one parse per token will systematically overstate certainty on exactly the constructions this lesson identifies
school-dependent: the preference principles are attributed to the classical grammarians as a tradition, and their relative ordering is not itself established by the lesson
rival analyses: the deleted-copula reading versus the plain circumstantial reading of the same string is presented as an open pair with no decision procedure beyond implied prior state
new_capability_required: A ranked_parse_set interface: the ability to emit several licensed analyses for one span with a preference ordering, the principle that produced the ordering, and an explicit abstention when context does not select. The listed capability families all assume a single verdict per item.
